body: {"total":7,"records":[{"title":"Diaries written by relatives versus usual care after prolonged mechanical ventilation: a randomised trial of post-traumatic stress symptoms at three months","authors":"Lindqvist-Obuya M, Harcourt-Ndiaye P, Sato-Brennan K","year":2019,"venue":"Journal of Intensive Care Aftercare","doi":"10.5555/jica.2019.0412","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Background: diaries kept during intensive care may help patients make sense of gaps in memory. Methods: 164 adults ventilated for at least 72 hours in three units were randomised to a diary written mainly by relatives with nurse support, or to usual care; the diary was read with the patient at a nurse visit one month after discharge. The primary outcome was a post-traumatic stress symptom score above the screening threshold at three months. Results: 14 of 81 patients in the diary group and 23 of 83 in the usual care group scored above the threshold (17 versus 28 percent). Anxiety and depression scores did not differ. Loss to follow-up was 19 percent. Conclusions: a relative-written diary was followed by fewer patients with high post-traumatic stress symptoms; the trial was not powered for secondary outcomes."},{"title":"Staff-written and family-written intensive care diaries: a systematic review of effects on psychological outcomes in patients and relatives","authors":"Ferreira-Abiodun C, Nakagawa-Holm T, Brandvold-Essien R, Mistry-Llorente A","year":2023,"venue":"Intensive Care Family Nursing Review","doi":"10.5555/ccnp.2023.0078","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We searched four databases to 2022 for controlled studies of intensive care diaries that reported post-traumatic stress, anxiety or depression in patients or relatives. Eleven studies, five of them randomised, were included. In patients, pooled post-traumatic stress symptoms were lower with diaries (standardised mean difference -0.31), but the effect was not seen when the three studies at high risk of bias were removed. In relatives, two studies reported fewer post-traumatic stress symptoms and one found no difference. Only three studies described diaries written mainly by families. Heterogeneity in the timing of diary reading and in outcome instruments was substantial, and certainty was rated low."},{"title":"Writing to someone who cannot answer: relatives' accounts of keeping a diary in intensive care","authors":"Okafor-Lindgren J, Varadi-Moss E","year":2021,"venue":"Nursing in Acute Care Settings","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We held in-depth conversations with 19 relatives who had kept a diary for a family member in intensive care. Relatives described the diary as a place to put fear and hope, and as something to do when they felt powerless at the bedside. Several stopped writing when the patient deteriorated and restarted only after discharge. Some worried about what the patient would think of entries written on the worst days, and four had removed pages before handing the diary over. Relatives valued a short guide and a nurse who asked about the diary; they disliked being told what to write. Findings come from one hospital and from relatives who agreed to talk."},{"title":"Distress on first reading an intensive care diary: an observational study of 96 survivors at a follow-up clinic","authors":"Achterberg-Salas N, Kowalewski-Otieno B, Dunmore-Ito H","year":2020,"venue":"Journal of Intensive Care Aftercare","doi":"10.5555/jica.2020.0233","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We asked 96 survivors to rate distress before and after first reading their diary with a nurse at a follow-up visit. Median distress rose from 2 to 4 on a 10-point scale during reading and returned to baseline within a week for 88 of 96 patients. Eight patients reported intrusive memories after reading, and six of them had high post-traumatic stress scores before reading. Photographs caused more distress than text for 21 patients. Reading with a nurse was preferred by 71 patients. The authors recommend screening for post-traumatic stress before the first reading and offering to hold back photographs until the patient asks for them."},{"title":"A family diary programme and post-traumatic stress symptoms in relatives: a before-after comparison in two units","authors":"Mbatha-Rousseau L, Grieve-Tanaka S","year":2017,"venue":"Intensive Care Family Nursing Review","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Two intensive care units introduced a diary programme in which relatives wrote daily with nurse prompts. We compared relatives of patients admitted in the 12 months before the change (n = 88) and the 12 months after it (n = 94), measuring post-traumatic stress symptoms 90 days after discharge or death. Symptoms above the screening threshold were reported by 36 percent of relatives before and 27 percent after. The difference was smaller when relatives of patients who died were excluded. Response to the 90-day questionnaire was 61 percent before and 58 percent after, and responders were more often spouses than adult children."},{"title":"Recommendations for intensive care diaries: a consensus statement from a regional critical care network","authors":"Regional Critical Care Network Diary Working Group","year":2024,"venue":"Regional Critical Care Network Reports","doi":"10.5555/rccn.2024.0015","providerType":"report","abstract":"A panel of 14 nurses, physicians, psychologists and former patients reviewed published studies and local experience of intensive care diaries and agreed nine recommendations over three modified Delphi rounds. The panel recommends offering diaries to patients ventilated for more than 72 hours, encouraging relatives to write, giving a short written guide, agreeing rules on photographs and confidentiality, and reading the diary with a trained clinician after discharge. It makes no recommendation on staff-written versus family-written entries because the evidence was judged insufficient. The panel notes that diary programmes often lapse when the lead nurse leaves the unit."},{"title":"Who receives an intensive care diary? Uptake by language, age and family presence across 1,120 eligible admissions","authors":"Haddad-Whitcombe R, Osei-Lundgren M, Petrov-Achebe D","year":2022,"venue":"Health Equity in Acute Care","doi":"10.5555/heac.2022.0147","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We reviewed diary uptake in 1,120 eligible admissions to four intensive care units over two years. A diary was started in 54 percent of admissions. Uptake was 31 percent when the family's main language differed from the unit's language, 38 percent for patients without a regular visitor, and 61 percent otherwise. Diaries were rarely offered to families who could visit only at night. Units with a named diary nurse had higher uptake than units without one. The authors recommend translated guides, an offer at the first family meeting, and recording who is offered a diary as well as who accepts it."}]}
